newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY JULY BUDGET DEFICIT SEEN ON TRACK FOR YEAR.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY JULY BUDGET DEFICIT SEEN ON TRACK FOR YEAR.

text.p: Hungary's central budget deficit for January to July keeps the country on track to meet its 1997 overall target despite higher than planned social security deficits, analysts said on Wednesday.
"The July figure can be considered good because it seems the government budget deficit target will be met," said Zoltan Varadi of Daewoo Securities.

According to finance ministry figures published on Tuesday, Hungary accumulated a central budget deficit of 188.9 billion forints in the first seven months of this year, up from the January-to-June figure of 165 billion, the finance ministry said in a statement on Tuesday.

The ministry targets a central state budget gap of 360 billion forints for 1997 and this week said its July prediction that the final figure would be 20 to 30 billion forints below the plan still stood.

However, Varadi said a spiralling social secirity deficit, which is accounted separately fron the central budget, was still a cause for concern, although extra tax revenues generated by a higher-than-planned increase this year in gross domestic product (GDP) should offset this.

The two social security funds, health and pension, are currently running a deficit well above the 13.5 billion forints budgeted for the year and the finance ministry has admitted that a 40-billion-forint deficit is likely.
However, the government says it will still meet its commitment to keep the overall 1997 budget deficit, including the social security and health funds, within 4.9 percent of GDP.

"The (360 billion forint) central budget projection was built on a lower GDP projection and I think (higher growth) can increase the tax revenues for the government so that the overall target is kept," Varadi said.
However, David Mars of SBC Warburg in London cautioned the Hungarian government against complacency over social spending.
"(The higher than expected growth) maybe masks the problem," he told Reuters.

"It could push inflation up and the budget deficit down and create the feeling that things aren't great but they're not that bad, such that in the next recession, in maybe our two, four or five years, not enough will have been done to rein in public spending on social welfare," he said.
"The government might be right in believing the economy can grow out of the problem, but thereagain they might not."
